To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) predation can be rational if the firm is threatened by many potential entrants, (2) the firm must be able to credibly commit to a future predatory policy, and (3) this credibility can be obtained through the firm's past actions.
Predatory practices are rational if a firm is under threat of entry, if it has an established reputation, and if the reputation is based on past behavior.

(1) predation may be a profitable entry deterrent when there is uncertainty about future competition, (2) predation may also be profitable even if it is not profitable in isolation, (3) the threat of predation may be credible even if it is never profitable in isolation, and (4) the threat of future predation may be used to deter entry even when there is no predation in the present.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the strategic use of reputation in a competitive environment.
the strategic interaction of firms with a common reputation, and with the role of reputation in the process of entry deterrence.
the question of whether a firm's reputation for predation is an asset or a liability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the analysis of reputation is an important and fruitful area of inquiry.
predation can be a rational response by a monopolist to the threat of competition, and that the threat of predation can deter entry.
predatory pricing is rational if the predator has a reputation for being a predator and if there are several potential entrants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
reputation is a useful tool to deter entry.
predation is rational if it is costly but not too costly, and if it is not too costly, it will be rational to deter predation.
reputation and predation are two sides of the same coin, and that they are both rational.
The main takeaway from our work is that
reputation can have an effect even when the firm's behavior is not observable.
the rationality of predation is intimately linked to the rationality of reputation.
the rationality of predatory pricing may be contingent on the firm's reputation and the nature of the market.
